This chowder isn’t just a soup

—it’s a warm, briny embrace from the Atlantic coast, filtered through the hands of a woman who knew how to make comfort elegant. Regina Victoria Zavecz’s 1999 recipe layers smoky bacon, tender clams, and sweet corn

into a creamy New England-style broth that’s both hearty and refined. The texture is velvety but never heavy, with bites of celery and corn offering gentle crunch, and the clams lending a briny chew that anchors the dish in its maritime roots.
The flavor profile is balanced and nostalgic: the salt of the sea, the sweetness of summer corn
and butter, and the quiet herbal lift of thyme and bay. A splash of dry sherry adds depth, hinting at the kind of kitchen where tradition meets a touch of flair.
Historically, clam chowder emerged from the fishing villages of the Northeast, where clams were plentiful and milk

was a pantry staple. But in our family, this version carries the initials RVZ—marking it not just as a regional classic, but as a personal one. Regina’s middle name, Victoria, passed down through Janiszewski women, speaks to resilience and grace. This chowder is one of her victories: a dish that turns humble ingredients into something worth remembering.
